As an optional extra, you can watch the sun rise over the coffee-growing valleys from a hot-air balloon. Departure is scheduled for around 5 a.m. and costs $1000 per person.

The main programme begins after breakfast. You'll travel to the Cocora Valley, one of the coffee region's best-known natural areas.

On arrival, you'll be welcomed with canelazo, a traditional drink. A specialist nature guide will then introduce you to the Cocora Nature Reserve.

After the walk, you'll continue into the palm forest. This is where the wax palm grows, Colombia's national tree and the tallest palm of its kind. Along the nature trail, you'll learn about local plants and wildlife and how Indigenous communities have historically regarded these trees.

The programme includes a symbolic ceremony honouring the Quindío wax palm and the planting of palm seedlings.

Optional activities in the valley include guided horseback rides through the countryside, routes through different parts of the valley, a traditional lunch at a restaurant at your own expense and a barista demonstration at Café Jesús Martín in Salento.

You'll then head into Salento itself. The walking tour takes you along colonial streets and past artisan workshops to the Cocora lookout. Transfer to your hotel at the scheduled time.
Horse riders among the green hills of the Cocora Valley, Colombia
Horseback riding through the green hills of the Cocora Valley

After breakfast, transfer to the airport for your flight to Medellín. The city tour begins on arrival.

Medellín is the capital of the department of Antioquia and one of Colombia's largest cities. You'll visit the Museum of Antioquia and Plaza Botero, where you can see sculptures and other works by Fernando Botero.

The tour continues to the Palace of Culture and Veracruz Church, both national monuments.

Part of the tour takes you through Comuna 13. Long associated with violence and drug wars, the district is now known for street art, graffiti and cultural projects.

The route also covers places associated with Pablo Escobar. The house where he died is in the Los Olivos neighbourhood. Accounts of the circumstances of his death differ. The route then takes in the ruins of the Dallas Building, where the inscription “Pablo vive!!!” remains, Montesacro Cemetery, where Escobar, his brother and his parents are buried, and the Mónaco Building.

Within Colombia, tours of this kind are controversial. City authorities oppose glorifying Escobar and seek to show a broader picture of modern Medellín beyond the legacy of the drug wars of the 1980s.

The tour ends at El Castillo Museum, built in 1930 and known for its art collections and gardens.
